summary: Defines additional optional DNS resource records for use with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP). It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

eli5.summary: The internet's phone book needs new kinds of entries for ILNP, which separates names from addresses. This memo adds those new entries. It is only an experiment.

questions: what dns records does ilnp need
what are the ilnp dns record types
what is the difference between nid and l64 records
subtitle: DNS records that separate a node's identity from its location.

tldr.problem: The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP) separates a node's permanent identifier from its network location (locator), but DNS records need new types to store and manage these split identifiers and locators.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four new DNS record types: NID (Node Identifier), L32 and L64 (32-bit and 64-bit locators), and LP (Locator Pointer), which DNS servers can store and return when queried by ILNP-capable nodes.
tldr.outcome: DNS can now help ILNP nodes discover each other's identifiers and locators, enabling mobility and multihoming without breaking existing sessions.

today: RFC 6742 is an Experimental Protocol. ILNP as a whole remains a research proposal and has not been widely deployed in the internet.

sections.title: Introduction to ILNP and DNS
sections.content:
The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP) is an experimental rethinking of how IP addresses work. Instead of using one address for both identity and location, ILNP splits them into two separate pieces: an Identifier that stays the same for a node, and a Locator that changes as the node moves. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the internet's main lookup service, but it was not designed with ILNP's split-address model in mind. This RFC describes new DNS record types needed to support ILNP.

These new records let DNS-aware nodes discover each other's identifiers and locators, enabling nodes to use ILNP for sessions even as they move between networks or gain multiple connections.
sections.eli5: DNS is like a phone book that stores addresses. ILNP splits each address into an identity part (who you are) and a location part (where you are). DNS needs new kinds of entries to store both pieces separately.

sections.title: The Four New Record Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines four new DNS resource record types for ILNP nodes:

NID (Node Identifier) records store a node's 64-bit Identifier. The record includes a 16-bit Preference field to let a node advertise which identifier it prefers when it has multiple identifiers.

L32 and L64 records store Locator values. L32 records hold 32-bit locators for ILNPv4-capable nodes, while L64 records hold 64-bit locators for ILNPv6-capable nodes. Each includes a Preference field and follows the syntax of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses respectively.

LP records (Locator Pointer) point to another DNS name, which can then be looked up to find L32 or L64 records. This provides indirection, useful when a multihomed site manages its locators centrally.
sections.eli5: NID is the identity part, like your name. L32 and L64 are location parts, like your street address. LP is like saying 'look up this other name to find my addresses'. Each one can be preferred over others.

sections.title: How DNS Queries and Preferences Work
sections.content:
When an ILNP-capable node queries DNS for another node, it can ask for NID, L32, L64, or LP records. DNS servers that understand ILNP (called ILNP-aware servers) can return related records in the Additional section of the response to reduce follow-up queries.

Preference values in these records indicate which identifier or locator the node prefers. Lower preference values are preferred. A node can have multiple NID, L32, L64, or LP records, allowing it to express preference among them. The record types can also be used as wildcards for subnets, pointing to a single DNS name that contains the actual locators for all hosts in that subnet.
sections.eli5: When you ask DNS 'where is Alice?', DNS can say 'Here is Alice's identity (NID), and here are her addresses (L64).' If Alice is at multiple addresses, she can say which one she prefers.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The simplest case is a single-homed ILNPv6 node: it has one NID record and one L64 record. If a node connects to two subnets (is multihomed), it has one NID record and multiple L64 records, each with different preference values.

For mobile networks, a node might have an NID record and an LP record pointing to a central location where its current locators are stored. This avoids updating the node's own DNS entry frequently; instead, only the central LP target needs updating when the node moves. The RFC notes that existing DNS servers that do not know about these new record types will handle them correctly as unknown record types, following RFC 3597.
sections.eli5: A stationary computer has one identity and one address. A laptop moving between offices has one identity but many addresses. A mobile user's phone always points to a central list that tracks where they are right now.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that these new DNS resource record types do not create new vulnerabilities in DNS. Existing DNS Security extensions (DNSSEC) can protect these records unchanged, authenticating that the records came from the right source and were not altered in transit. If these records are updated dynamically over the network, the Secure Dynamic DNS Update mechanism (RFC 3007) should be used.

IANA allocated specific type values: NID is 104, L32 is 105, L64 is 106, and LP is 107. These values are registered in the DNS resource record type registry.
sections.eli5: DNS records can be forged, but existing security tools lock them down. New addresses stored this way can be protected the same way as existing DNS records.
